title: 7 Signs Your EAP Needs a Modern Upgrade
summary: Low EAP utilization, long wait times, and limited data signal it may be time to modernize. Learn how HR leaders can evaluate and update their EAP.
body_markdown:
Your employee assistance program (EAP) might offer a 24/7 helpline, a large provider network, and short-term counseling. But how easy is it for employees to get the help they need?


Traditional EAPs provide valuable support, especially during a crisis or difficult period. Yet employees seeking help often face long provider searches, limited care options, and confusing referrals. Some give up before they ever receive support.


You can track how many employees use your EAP, but that number won't tell you how easy it was for them to get care, whether they got the support they needed, or what happened when they needed more help.


If you're evaluating your current EAP or considering an upgrade, these seven signs deserve a closer look.
‍


## 1. Utilization stays low despite ongoing promotion
‍


You've sent the emails, reminded managers about the benefit, and included EAP information in open enrollment materials. Employees still aren't using it.


There's no universal utilization benchmark that defines a successful EAP. Programs measure participation differently, and engagement depends on workforce needs, eligibility, awareness, trust, and the services available.


Still, persistently low use calls for a closer look at the employee experience.


Some employees worry about confidentiality or feel uncomfortable seeking support through work. Others don't understand what the benefit covers or see services that fit their needs. A confusing intake process can also discourage someone from taking the first step.


More promotion won't fix a benefit that's difficult to use.


Start by looking beyond the overall utilization rate. Examine which groups engage, what services they use, and where employees drop out of the process. Compare patterns across regions and eligible populations. Employee feedback can help identify barriers that utilization reports miss.
‍


## 2. Getting care takes too much time and effort
‍


An employee decides to seek mental health support. They open the provider directory, contact several clinicians, and wait for responses. Some providers aren't accepting new patients. Others don't accept the employee's insurance or have no appointments available.


By the time the employee finds someone, days or weeks have passed.


That process takes time and energy from anyone seeking support. For someone already dealing with depression, anxiety, or severe stress, it can be especially difficult.


A large provider network means little if employees struggle to find someone who is available and meets their needs.


**Look beyond appointment wait times to measure how long it takes employees to reach care.** Some programs start the clock when an appointment is scheduled, leaving out the time employees spend searching for a provider or following up on referrals.


Review the full experience, from the first request for help to the first appointment. Find out how the program assesses employee needs, keeps provider information current, and handles unsuccessful matches. Employees should have a clear path forward when the first option doesn't work.
‍


## 3. Reporting tells you who's using the EAP, but little else
‍


Your EAP reports how many employees used the program, how many sessions they attended, and which services were most popular.


That's useful information. But it leaves major questions unanswered.


Did employees get support that fit their needs? How long did it take? Were they satisfied with their care? Did their mental health improve?


To evaluate what you're paying for, look for reporting that includes:


- **Engagement:** Who uses the benefit, which services they choose, and how participation changes over time
- **Access:** How quickly employees connect with support and where they encounter delays
- **Employee experience:** Whether employees find services useful and appropriate for their needs
- **Outcomes:** Changes in clinical symptoms or well-being, when appropriate and measurable
- **Workforce trends:** Differences in engagement and access across regions or eligible populations, where sample sizes allow


Reporting also has limits. Privacy requirements, local regulations, and minimum reporting thresholds restrict what employers can see. Some services may use different measurement methods.


The goal is to gather enough reliable information to understand how the benefit performs and where it needs improvement.
‍


## 4. Global coverage doesn't translate into consistent access
‍


Your EAP vendor says it supports employees in dozens of countries. What does that coverage look like for someone trying to get help in each location?


An employee in the U.S. might have access to several types of care and a broad provider network. Someone in another country may face fewer options, different referral processes, or limited support in their preferred language.


Some differences are unavoidable. Provider availability, regulations, clinical practices, and cultural expectations vary across markets.


Still, employers need to know what employees can expect in each location.


**Evaluate the experience country by country.** Examine which services are available, how employees find local providers, what languages are supported, and how the program handles needs that fall outside its coverage.


A single global coverage figure won't reveal these differences.


*Related reading:*[How to Consolidate Global EAP Services Without Losing What Works](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/how-to-consolidate-global-eap-services-without-losing-what-works) *↗ ‍*


## 5. Employees can't find support that fits their needs and preferences
‍


Finding mental health care involves more than locating an available appointment.


Employees may prefer a provider who speaks their language, understands their cultural background, specializes in a particular concern, or offers appointments outside traditional business hours.


Those preferences affect how comfortable someone feels seeking help and whether they continue with care.


In[a KFF survey](https://www.kff.org/racial-equity-and-health-policy/racial-and-ethnic-disparities-in-mental-health-care-findings-from-the-kff-survey-of-racism-discrimination-and-health/) , 41% of adults who received or tried to find mental health care for themselves or a child said it was somewhat or very difficult to find a provider who could understand and relate to their background and experiences.


Provider choice is only part of the equation. Employees also have different preferences for the *type* of support they receive.


A[RAND Europe study](https://explore.modernhealth.com/global-coverage-site/global-engagement-study) of more than 178,000 registered Modern Health members found differences in care use across regions. Members in Asia used more self-guided digital resources and fewer one-on-one sessions. U.S. members showed the opposite pattern.


These findings show why offering only one or two ways to engage can limit a program's appeal and usefulness.


Some employees need therapy or specialty care. Others benefit from coaching, group support, or self-guided resources. The best starting point depends on their needs, goals, and preferences.


Look for a program that offers appropriate choices and helps employees understand their options. They shouldn't have to figure out which type of care they need on their own.
‍


## 6. Employees are left on their own when counseling sessions run out
‍


An employee reaches the end of their covered EAP counseling sessions. They're making progress, but they still need support.


What happens next?


Traditional EAPs typically offer a set number of counseling sessions. Session limits are also common in other employer-sponsored mental health benefits. The limit itself doesn't tell you whether the program is effective.


**What happens when an employee reaches that limit tells you much more.**


Employees who need continued care may receive a referral to their health plan, a community provider, or another service. But a referral that sends someone back to the beginning of a provider search creates another barrier.


They may have to explain their concerns again, find a clinician who accepts their coverage, or wait weeks for an appointment.


Review how your EAP manages these transitions. Does it identify when someone needs continued care? Are employees told about coverage limits early? Does the program help them connect with the next provider or service?


Every benefit has coverage boundaries. Employees need clear guidance and a practical next step when they reach them.
‍


## 7. Support is available during a crisis, but harder to access before one
‍


Crisis services are a core part of an EAP. Employees need dependable access to urgent help, and organizations need support when critical incidents affect the workplace.


Yet mental health needs don't always begin with a crisis.


An employee might be struggling with a growing workload, a difficult life transition, family caregiving, or ongoing stress. They may want to develop coping skills, improve relationships, or get support before their symptoms become more severe.


If the EAP's most visible services are a crisis hotline and short-term counseling, employees may assume the benefit isn't meant for these needs.


Offering different ways to engage helps employees seek support earlier.


For example, coaching can help employees work toward personal goals, manage everyday challenges, and build coping skills. Group sessions and digital resources can make it easier to learn new strategies or connect with others. Therapy and specialty care provide support for clinical needs.


The program should also help employees move between services when their needs change.


An employee who starts with coaching may later need therapy. Someone completing treatment may benefit from continued support through coaching or self-guided resources.


The goal is to make it easy for employees to find appropriate support at different stages of need, without having to start over each time.
‍


## What to look for when evaluating your EAP
‍


Finding one of these warning signs doesn't automatically mean you need to replace your EAP. It does mean there's room to improve how the benefit supports your workforce.


For some employers, the priority will be faster access to care or better provider matching. Others may need more support options, stronger global coverage, clearer reporting, or help connecting employees with continued care.


Start with the areas that create the most friction for employees. Work with your current vendor to understand what's causing those problems and which changes are possible within your existing plan.


Then evaluate whether your current EAP can meet your workforce's needs or whether it's time to expand your mental health benefits.


Look for a solution that makes it easier for employees to get started, offers care that fits different needs, supports transitions between services, and gives you reliable evidence of how the benefit performs.
